summary:
Titus was one of Paul's most seasoned coworkers, a Gentile believer trusted with hard assignments, and Paul has left him on the island of Crete to finish organizing its new churches: appoint elders in every town, and silence teachers who "for the sake of dishonorable gain... undermine entire households" (1:11). Crete's reputation preceded it; Paul quotes one of the island's own poets, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons" (1:12), and does not dispute the assessment.

The elder qualifications in chapter 1 are about character, not talent, set against the "empty talk and deception" (1:10) already at work. Chapter 2 then shows what sound teaching looks like when people live it, group by group — older men, older women, the young, slaves — so that in every respect "they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior" (2:10). In this letter, doctrine is something behavior makes either attractive or unbelievable.

Twice Titus compresses the gospel into a few lines, among the clearest such summaries in the New Testament: grace "has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone," and it "instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions" (2:11-12); God "saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy" (3:5). Short as it is, the letter keeps belief and behavior in a single frame; watch how every passage moves between the two.
